Effect of microaeration combined with ferric chloride pretreatment 
on anaerobic digestion of corn stalk
Zhiqiang Wanga, Jinming Liub, and Feng Tanb
aCollege of Engineering, Heilongjiang Bayi Agricultural University, Daqing, P. R. China; bCollege of Information and 
Electrical Engineering, Heilongjiang Bayi Agricultural University, Daqing, P. R. China
ABSTRACT
In this study, microaeration combined with ferric chloride pretreatment was 
used to improve the methanogenic performance for thermophilic dry anae­
robic digestion. Parameter optimization and mechanism analysis were 
explored for combined pretreatment in anaerobic digestion by response 
surface methodology and microbial diversity and community. The results 
showed that both microaeration and ferric chloride had significant effects on 
the cumulative methane production, and the effect of microaeration was 
greater than that of ferric chloride. The optimal pretreatment parameters 
were predicted at oxygen loading rate of 0.76 mL/g VS and ferric chloride 
addition rate of 4.04 mg/g VS. The methane production of anaerobic diges­
tion was 114.05 mL/g VS with the optimal pretreatment parameters, which 
was 17.78% higher than that without pretreatment. In addition, microbial 
community analysis showed that combined pretreatment enhanced metha­
nogenesis by enhancing the hydrogenotrophic pathway.

Introduction
Anaerobic digestion is a green biotechnology that converts organic matter from waste into methane 
(Wang, Li, and Yu et al. 2022). At present, there are mainly three categories of wet, semi-dry, and dry 
anaerobic digestion, whose TS is ≤10%, 10–15%, and ≥15%, respectively (Zhen, Luo, and Xing et al. 
2021). Among them, semi-dry or dry anaerobic digestion has not been widely promoted due to the 
lack of adequate technology to keep the digestive system running steadily compared to wet anaerobic 
digestion (Deepanraj, Senthilkumar, and Ranjitha 2021). Some problems such as poor fluidity and 
mass transfer of feedstock and low stability of the digestive system remain to be solved in dry 
anaerobic digestion, which leads to excessive accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) or ammonia 
nitrogen (Esen and Yuksel 2013; Rocamora, Wagland, and Villa et al. 2020). However, greater TS, less 
digestate generation, smaller digesters, and higher biogas production make semi-dry and dry anaero­
bic digestion more attractive.
In view of the existing problems of dry anaerobic digestion, several methods, such as temperature 
adjustment, pretreatment, and additives, have been tried from the two main processes of anaerobic 
digestion, namely, hydrolytic acidification and methane production (Kainthola, Kalamdhad, and 
Goud 2019b; Sun, Wang, and Liu et al. 2020a). In general, microbial activity is stimulated through 
ambient temperature, thereby shortening the digestion cycle and increasing the organic load rate (Nie, 
He, and Zhang et al. 2021). Some facultative bacteria that release proteolytic and cellulolytic enzymes 
are propagated by microaeration (MA) pretreatment, which can improve the hydrolytic acidification 
process (Amin, Khalid, and Li et al. 2021). The addition of trace elements is also a convenient way to 
adjust the stability of dry anaerobic digestion, which can accelerate the growth of methanogens (Yu,

Zhang, and Dai et al. 2016). Some trace elements (such as Fe, Co, and Ni) have been shown to be 
essential nutrients needed for the growth of methanogens (e.g. methyl-coenzyme M and coenzyme 
M methyl-transferase) (Zhang, Wu, and Guo et al. 2015). Moreover, Fe is one of the most needed 
metal elements for microorganisms, which can accept/donate electrons in the redox reaction, so as to 
improve microbial activity and accelerate substrate hydrolysis (Ugwu and Enweremadu 2020). 
However, a single potential improvement method often has bottlenecks and limitations that are 
difficult to break. It seems feasible to integrate multiple processes to optimize the performance of 
dry anaerobic digestion.
Conventionally, “one at a time” variation of variables is applied to the optimization of many 
industrial processes, in which the response variable is only a function of a single variable parameter, 
and the processing parameters are assumed to be non-interacting (Ahmadi, Vahabzadeh, and 
Bonakdarpour et al. 2005). When multiple independent variables interact together to affect the desired 
response, the response surface methodology (RSM) can effectively optimize and evaluate the process 
(Kainthola, Kalamdhad, and Goud 2019a). Therefore, RSM provides a set of analysis and solution 
programs for many industrial process problems, such as optimal product design, process improve­
ment, and system optimization (Gunes, Stokes, and Davis et al. 2021).
Based on the above analysis, the effects of microaeration combined with ferric chloride (MAFC) 
pretreatment on thermophilic anaerobic digestion of corn stalk (CS) were investigated. The specific 
purposes of this study were: (1) To optimize the optimal conditions of MAFC pretreatment and 
explore the effect of pretreatment conditions on cumulative methane production (CMP) by central 
composite design (CCD); (2) To reveal the enhancement mechanism of MAFC pretreatment on 
anaerobic digestion performance through microbial diversity and community.
Materials and Methods
Substrate and inoculum
The characteristics of CS and inoculum are listed in Table 1. CS was collected from a farm in 
Heilongjiang, China, which was air-dried and crushed to nearly 1 cm by a pulverizer, and then stored 
at room temperature. The inoculum was derived from a 10 L mesophilic anaerobic digester.
Experimental design
Central composite design
The CCD is used to convert two independent variables into dimensionless variables (x1, x2), whose 
coded values are of five levels: −a, −1, 0, +1, +a. Based on the results of the pre-experiment, the actual 
representation and magnitude order for the coded value were assigned and listed in Table 2. According 
to the CCD arrangement in Table 3, the experiment required 13 runs, and all experimental and 
predicted values are listed. Then, the evaluation of lack of fitness and experimental error was carried 
out through the central operation.

MAFC pretreatment
According to the CCD arrangement, different conditions of MAFC pretreatment were satisfied. 
Firstly, 50 g CS, 75 mL deionized water, and 200 mL inocula were mixed in each 500 mL serum vial. 
Then, different proportions of ferric chloride (FC) reagents were added to the serum vial. FC reagents 
of 0, 0.88, 3, 5.12, and 6 mg/g VS were added to different serum vials to form different mass ratios of 
FC and CS. A certain proportion of oxygen (0, 0.44, 1.5, 2.56, and 3 mL/g VS) was slowly injected into 
the bottom of different serum vials through a syringe during the anaerobic digestion process each day 
to form a microoxygen environment with different loads.
Anaerobic digestion experiments
The anaerobic digestion experiment was divided into two parts. The first part was used to evaluate the 
CMP of different MAFC pretreatments in an automated biomethane potential test system with 15 
channel reactors (AMPTSII, Bioprocess Control, Lund, Sweden). The system consists of a digestion 
unit, a CO2 removal unit, and a gas flow measurement unit, which enables on-line monitoring of 
biomethane. All serum vials were digested at 36°C for 25 days with a blender at 50 rpm.
The second part is to explore the potential mechanism of MAFC pretreatment to improve the 
anaerobic digestion performance. Firstly, the optimal pretreatment conditions should be determined 
based on the CMP results of anaerobic digestion and the optimization of RSM. Then, the two serum

vials were retested for anaerobic digestion to compare and analyze performance differences. One was 
pretreated with optimum MAFC conditions and the other was not pretreated (CK). In addition, daily 
methane production was monitored to assess the biomethane performance of anaerobic digestion. 
Digested substrates were collected at the beginning, middle, and end of anaerobic digestion for the 
impact of MAFC on the microbial community by 16S rRNA sequencing. Three parallel replicates were 
performed to ensure repeatability of the experiment.
Analytical Methods
The APHA standard method was used for TS and VS in the samples. The lignocellulose component 
contents (hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin) were measured according to the Van Soest method. The 
C and N contents of the samples were analyzed by the elemental analyzer (EA 3000, LEEMAN 
Technologies Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). The experimental data was analyzed by Origin 2017 (Origin 
Lab Corporation, Northampton, MA, USA), and the RSM was done on Design Expert 10.0 (Stat-Ease 
Inc., US).
Microbial diversity and community
The microbial community was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing technology. To analyze the 
system state of anaerobic digestion, digestive samples were collected for DNA extraction on day 5, 15 
and 25, respectively. The universal primers were used to amplify the bacterial 16S rRNA sequence 
fragment. Sequencing was analyzed on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, USA). 
Operational taxonomic unit (OUT) clustering was analyzed by Ribosomal Database Project (RDP) 
database (http://rdp.cme.msu.edu/).

Results and discussion
Diagnostic checking and statistical analysis of the model
In this study, the effect of MAFC pretreatment parameters (oxygen load and FC ratio) on CMP was 
investigated by CCD. After applying several regression investigations, a second-order polynomial 
equation representing the correlation between the two pretreatment parameters and CMP in was 
simulated by multiple regression analysis of the experimental data. Therefore, the regression model in 
response to CMP based on coded and uncoded factors was as follows

A good statistical model should have an R2 value in the range of 0.75–1, which will guide the best fit of 
the model (Kainthola, Kalamdhad, and Goud 2019a). The R2 of this model was 0.9223, indicating that 
92.23% variability in the CMP response can be explained. Statistical parameters obtained from the 
analysis of variance (ANOVA) for the adequacy and significance of the regression model are given in 
Table 4. The F value and p-value of the quadratic model were 16.61 and 0.0009 (<0.01), respectively, 
which meant the quadratic model was significant. The lack of fit value was 22.43 (p = 0.0770, not 
significant), implying that it was significantly relative to the pure error. Additionally, the effect of MA 
on CMP was greater than that of FC due to the larger F value (Wang, Cheng, and Liu et al. 2019a), and 
they were significant for CMP (p < .05).
To check the adequacy of the model, diagnostic model items were calculated, and standardized 
residuals showed slight differences between the hypothetical model items and the response model 
items. In Figures S1, normal probability plots of standardized residuals and actual and predicted CMP 
curves were shown. The more balls are distributed on the slash, the better the confidence is shown for 
the model. The results showed that there was no anomaly in the experiment, and the expectation of 
CMP enhancement was obtained through the quadratic model.
Effect of MAFC pretreatment on CMP
As shown in Figure 1(a), when the addition ratio of FC was 3 mg/g VS (central level), CMP gradually 
increased with microaeration pretreatment. However, a downward trend was shown in the CMP at 
oxygen loading rates in excess of 0.43–0.86 mL/g VS. This result was consistent with studies by Fu, 
Wang, and Yuan et al. (2015) who showed that moderate aeration could improve CMP. They 
confirmed that the CMP for anaerobic digestion of CS was increased by 16.2% at oxygen load of 
5 mL/g VS. The microoxygen environment is conducive to the metabolism of aerobic and facultative 
anaerobic microorganisms, which increases the content of cellulose, protein, and other hydrolytic 
enzymes to promote the hydrolysis of complex organic compounds (Brémond, de Buyer, and Steyer 
et al. 2018). However, the activity of anaerobic methanogens is inhibited by toxicity at higher oxygen 
levels, which will compete with facultative microorganisms on the substrates (Xu, Selvam, and Wong 
2014). Thus, excessive aeration has a negative effect on CMP during anaerobic digestion (Lim and 
Wang 2013). In addition, rapid hydrolysis of substrates may lead to excessive accumulation of VFA, 
resulting in inhibition of anaerobic digestion (Sheets, Ge, and Li 2015). Zhen, Luo, and Xing et al. 
(2021) found that the increased butyric acid content exceeded 8 g/L with the excess oxygen load, which 
led to the inhibition of dry anaerobic digestion.

Figure 1(b) shows that a higher FC addition rate resulted in a higher CMP (Oxygen load was 
retained at its central level). This is due to the fact that FC can be used as an electron acceptor to 
accelerate complex organic hydrolysis and promote the bioconversion of reducing sugars and amino 
acids to acetic acid by the acquisition of intermediate electrons (Zhan, Tian, and Zhang et al. 2021). 
Zhao, Li, and Zhao et al. (2020) also reported that dissimilated iron reduction was the primary route to 
improve the methanogenic performance of FC pretreatment. The Fe(III)-reducing microorganisms 
could be enriched by the addition of ferric chloride and the use of Fe(III) as an electron acceptor to 
promote organic decomposition via the DIR process (Baek, Kim, and Lee 2014). Another explanation 
is that the supplementation of ferric chloride can enrich Coprothermobacter for proteins fermentation 
and Methanosarcina for methanogenesis (Yu, Lou, and Zhang et al. 2015a). However, the limited 
increase in the CMP even began to be inhibited as the FC reached 3–4.5 mg/g VS. This result was 
similar to the study of Zhan, Tian, and Zhang et al. (2021), and the FC dosage below 390 mg Fe(III)/L 
would not bring a huge shock to the anaerobic digestive. Due to excessive FC supplementation, pH 
decreased sharply along with the rapid hydrolysis of FC (Eq. (6)), which may impair methanogen 
activity and thus give rise to a poor CMP (Qin, Chen, and Wang et al. 2019).

In summary, restricted oxygen increased the hydrolysis rate of the substrate, but it also faced the 
potential problem of excessive accumulation caused by rapid VFA generation. On the other hand, 
although high Fe concentrations caused digestive system collapse, appropriate FC supplementation 
accelerated VFA conversion and promoted methanogen activity, which prevented excessive accumu­
lation of VFA formed by rapid substrate hydrolysis and improved methane production efficiency. 
Therefore, a high CMP could be obtained by MAFC pretreatment. From Figure 2, the 3D model 
showed that the maximum predicted CMP was obtained at oxygen loading rate of 0.76 mL/g VS and 
ferric chloride addition rate of 4.04 mg/g VS, which can be used as optimized pretreatment conditions 
for subsequent studies.
Methane production performance during dry anaerobic digestion
Figure 3(a) shows the daily methane production of anaerobic digestion for raw and MAFC pretreated 
CS. CK obtained methane production of 2.64 mL/g VS, which was 105.47% higher than that of the 
MAFC pretreatment on the first day. As the anaerobic environment was destroyed by MAFC 
pretreatment, the activity of methanogens was inhibited to a certain extent. Afterward, daily methane

production for MAFC pretreatment gradually increased and exceeded the daily methane production 
for CK by day 3, which can be attributed to the fast hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and methanogenesis 
(Chen, Yang, and Zhao et al. 2019a). In the following days, daily methane production remained at 
a high level in both groups and peaked on the fifth day. A maximum daily methane production of 
16.25 mL/g VS was obtained for MAFC, which was 34.19% higher than that for CK (12.11 mL/g VS). 
In addition, after 13 days of anaerobic digestion, the daily methane production of CK was again higher 
than that of MAFC, due to the accelerated hydrolysis rate and rapid substrate depletion caused by 
MAFC pretreatment. Eventually, the CMP detected was 114.05 mL/g VS for MAFC, exceeding 17.78% 
of CMP for CK (Figure 3(b)).
In order to compare the hydrolytic and methanogenic performance of anaerobic digestion before 
and after MAFC, first-order kinetic model and modified Gompertz model were applied to fit the 
profiles of CMP (Xu, Awasthi, and Li et al. 2020). The high coefficient (R2 > 0.945) of all fittings 
indicates that the model curves were reliable. The hydrolysis constant (k) can reflect the hydrolysis rate 
of the digested substrate, and the higher the p value, the better the hydrolysis property (Chen, Zhu, and 
Jiang et al. 2019b). It is evident that the hydrolysis rate of the substrate was increased by MAFC 
pretreatment (Table 5). In addition, the lag-phase time (λ) of MAFC increased by 34.29% compared 
with CK (1.40). Longer λ indicates slower adaptation to the anaerobic digestion as well as lower CMP

Analysis of microbial community composition and diversity
Anaerobic digestion is a multistage biochemical process in which many kinds of microorganisms act 
together. The influence of MAFC pretreatment on anaerobic digestion performance can be analyzed 
by the changes of microbial diversity and community at different times (Sepehri and Sarrafzadeh 
2018). Therefore, the diversity and structure were evaluated in the 5th, 15th, and 25th days of 
anaerobic digestion.
Effects of MAFC pretreatment on microbial diversity
Alpha diversity reflects the species diversity of a single sample. The ACE and Chao1 index are used to 
estimate the total number of species in the sample, and the higher the value, the more species. Shannon 
and Simpson indexes are commonly used to reflect the diversity of alpha. The higher the Shannon 
value is, the higher the community diversity is, while the Simpson value is the opposite. From Table 6, 
the sequence numbers of CK were 45221–72453 for bacteria and 48967–55216 for archaea, with a total 
of 1143–1782 and 532–631 OTUs detected for bacteria and archaea at day 5, 15, and 25, respectively. 
Whereas the sequence numbers of MAFC were 48346−72950 for bacteria and 56085−58822 for 
archaea, with a total of 1031−2113 and 597–683 OTUs detected for bacteria and archaea, respectively. 
Higher Alpha diversity reflects better ecological stability and higher toxicity resistance during anae­
robic digestion (Lu, Xing, and Ren 2012). Therefore, the application of MAFC pretreatment improved 
the stability of the anaerobic digestion system. In addition, the changes in ACE, Chao1, Shannon, and 
Simpson indexes also confirmed that MAFC was beneficial to the stability of anaerobic digestion.

Effects of MAFC pretreatment on microbial community
As shown in Figure 4(a), four dominant phyla, namely Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Synergistetes, and 
Proteobacteria, were identified in anaerobic digestion. Firmicutes accounted for the largest propor­
tion in the whole process of anaerobic digestion that mainly released lipases, proteases, and 
cellulases that hydrolyze organic matter (Cai, Hua, and Gao et al. 2017). Bacteroidetes dominates 
the conversion of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins to VFA (Wang, Zhang, and Zhou et al. 2017). 
Synergistetes and Proteobacteria play a leading role in the conversion of VFA to acetic acid/ 
hydrogen, which can be used to feed the aceticlastic and hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Jiang, 
Li, and Li et al. 2020).
On the 5th day of anaerobic digestion, the relative abundances of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, 
Synergistetes, and Proteobacteria in CK were 95.73%, 1.15%, 1.71%, and 0.89%, respectively. In 
contrast, only the relative abundance of Firmicutes decreased in MAFC (90.17%), while the 
relative abundance of Bacteroidetes, Synergistetes, and Proteobacteria increased by 234.78%, 
248.89%, and 92.13%, respectively. Previous reports have shown that MA provided a suitable 
oxygen environment to accelerate the growth of facultative bacteria, which was conducive to 
their absorption of small molecule compounds to release VFA (Charles, Walker, and Cord- 
Ruwisch 2009; Sun, Zhang, and Sun et al. 2020b). While, Yu, Shan, and Zhang et al. (2015b) also 
found that the addition of FC could inhibit excessive VFA synthesis and maintain system 
stability. Thus, MAFC pretreatment could balance the stability of the system while accelerating 
the acidogenic phase, that is, the conversion of small molecule compounds to VFA and further 
acetic acid/hydrogen. On the 15th day, the relative abundance of Firmicutes pretreated by MAFC 
was 7.10% higher than that of CK, while the other three phyla were lower than that of CK, 
indicating that the acidogenic phase was weakened for the MAFC group compared with CK. 
This result is supported by the above trends in daily methane production. On the 25th day, there 
was little difference in relative abundance of the digestive system before and after MAFC 
pretreatment on the bacterial phylum level.
Figure 4(b) depicts the relative abundance of bacterial communities at genus level on the 5th day. 
Six genera with high relative abundances were individually figured, and they were Sinibacillus, 
Tepidimicrobium, Clostridium III, Dethiobacter, Tisierella, and Bacillus. Clostridium was the most 
abundant genus of bacteria for CK and MAFC with relative abundances of 16.36% and 20.66%, 
respectively. It is a typical hydrolytic and acidogenic genus of bacteria in thermophilic anaerobic 
digestion. Also, a higher relative abundance of Clostridium for MAFC meant a better rate of hydrolysis 
during the prophase of digestion (Ziganshin, Liebetrau, and Pr?Ter 2013). The relative abundance of

Sinibacillus significantly increased after MAFC pretreatment on day 15, while that of CK changed 
little. The increase of the relative abundance of Sinibacillus, a facultative thermophilic bacterium with 
the function of degrading organic matter, might be caused by early MA. In addition, the proportion of 
Tepidimicrobium is seen as an indicator of the acidification process, its relative abundance in MAFC 
was lower than that in CK throughout anaerobic digestion, suggesting that the former has a more 
stable digestive system (Regueiro, Lema, and Carballa 2015).
Several major archaea were identified and listed in Figure 5. There were five hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens, 
namely, 
Methanobacterium, 
Methanomassiliicoccus, 
Methanosphaera, 
Methanobrevibacter, and Methanolinea, which metabolize hydrogen and carbon dioxide to pro­
duce methane (Capson-Tojo, Moscoviz, and Astals et al. 2020). As the only acetoclastic archaea in 
this study, Methanothrix played a dominant role, and its relative abundance increased with time. 
Dissimilarly, the relative abundances of Methanothrix in MAFC were 9.66%, 49.94%, and 45.12% 
lower than that of CK on day 5, 15, and 25, respectively. The results showed that MAFC 
pretreatment was not suitable for the growth and reproduction of Methanothrix. It has been 
reported that acetoclastic methanogens were more sensitive to environmental changes than 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Lü, Hao, and Guan et al. 2013). Thus, MAFC pretreatment 
enhanced methanogenesis by enhancing the hydrogenotrophic pathway.
Conclusions
This study demonstrated that MAFC pretreatment promoted the methanogenic properties of 
thermophilic dry anaerobic digestion. Both MA and FC had significant effects on CMP, and the 
optimal pretreatment parameters were: oxygen loading rate of 0.76 mL/g VS and FC addition 
rate of 4.04 mg/g. The CMP of MAFC pretreatment was 114.05 mL/g VS with the optimal 
conditions, which was 17.78% higher than that of CK. In addition, microbial community analysis 
showed that MAFC pretreatment enhanced methanogenesis by enhancing the hydrogenotrophic 
pathway. The success of this pretreatment provides a potential way to improve the performance 
of dry anaerobic digestion.
